title: THE FIRST CITY IN THE BIBLE WAS BUILT BY A MURDERER’S SON—BUT THE NAME BEHIND IT REVEALS SOMETHING EVEN MORE DISTURBING
paragraphs: THE FIRST CITY IN THE BIBLE WAS BUILT BY A MURDERER’S SON—BUT THE NAME BEHIND IT REVEALS SOMETHING EVEN MORE DISTURBING

Before there was Babylon, before there were kings and kingdoms, a father with blood on his hands watched his son become the namesake of the first city mentioned in Scripture. But Genesis 4:16–17 reveals something far deeper than an ancient family history. It confronts the terrifying possibility of building an impressive life while living far from God.
There is something unsettling about the first city mentioned in the Bible.
Not because of its walls.
Not because of its buildings.
Not because of how many people might have lived there.
But because of the man who built it.
And the father whose name was already stained by the blood of his own brother.

Before humanity ever heard of Jerusalem, before the rise of Egypt, before the towers of Babylon, Scripture introduces a city connected to a family carrying one of the darkest stories in human history.
And what makes this account so uncomfortable is that the people involved were not strangers to God.
They knew something about Him.
They had heard His voice.
They had experienced His warnings.
And still, one of them chose a path that would forever change human history.
The question seems simple.
Who was the father of the man who built the first city mentioned in Scripture?
The answer is Cain.
Yes. That Cain.
The man who murdered Abel.
The man who became angry when God did not regard his offering as He regarded his brother's.
The man whom God warned before the murder.
The man who later heard the Lord ask him a question no guilty conscience could comfortably answer:
"Where is Abel thy brother?" (Genesis 4:9, KJV)
But there is a detail here that deserves careful attention.
Genesis 4:17 does not actually say Cain's son built the city.
It says Cain himself built the city and named it after his son, Enoch.
That distinction matters.
Because the story is not simply about a son inheriting a father's shame.
It is about a father attempting to establish a future after committing an irreversible act.
And somewhere in that ancient story is a warning for every person who has ever tried to build something beautiful while avoiding something broken inside.
Read the passage carefully.
"And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod, on the east of Eden.
"And Cain knew his wife; and she conceived, and bare Enoch: and he builded a city, and called the name of the city, after the name of his son, Enoch." (Genesis 4:16–17, KJV)
At first glance, it sounds almost ordinary.
A man moves to another land.
He has a family.
He builds a city.
He names it after his child.
But when you remember what happened immediately before these verses, the entire atmosphere changes.
Because Cain did not simply move away from his childhood home.
He went out from the presence of the LORD.
And those words should make us uncomfortable.
Not because God suddenly became unable to see Cain.
Not because Cain could escape the Creator's authority.
But because the narrative portrays a man departing from the place of direct encounter with God after judgment for his sin.
The Hebrew of Genesis 4:16 says:
וַיֵּצֵא קַיִן מִלִּפְנֵי יְהוָה
Vayyetse Qayin millifnei Adonai.

Literally, the expression communicates that Cain went out from before the presence, or face, of the LORD. The written divine name is represented by יהוה (YHWH), traditionally read aloud as Adonai in Jewish practice.
There is a heartbreaking contrast here.
Cain had heard God's voice.
Cain had received God's warning.
Cain had been confronted about his sin.
And now the narrative describes him going away.
Think about that.
The same God who warned Cain before he murdered Abel was the God who questioned him afterward.
Before the bloodshed, God said:
"If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him." (Genesis 4:7, KJV)
Sin was at the door.
Cain had a warning.
He was not left without moral responsibility.
Yet he opened the door.
And Abel died.
Somebody reading this knows what it feels like to look back at a moment when you knew better.
You saw the warning signs.
You felt the conviction.
You knew the words you were about to say would wound someone.
You knew the secret you were protecting was beginning to control you.
You knew the resentment was becoming dangerous.
But you kept feeding it.
And eventually, something broke.
Maybe not a human life, as in Cain's terrible crime.
Maybe it was trust.
A marriage.
A friendship.
A testimony.
A relationship with someone who once believed you would never hurt them.
And afterward, you tried to move forward.
You worked harder.
You stayed busy.
You made plans.
You tried to become someone different.
But the thing you had not honestly faced kept following you.
That is one reason Cain's story remains so haunting.
He built a city.
But Scripture never says that building the city healed his heart.
It never says the buildings erased Abel's blood.
It never says his achievements amounted to repentance.
And it never says that naming a city after his son restored his fellowship with God.
We must not pretend to know Cain's private motives. Genesis does not explicitly tell us whether he built the city out of fear, ambition, affection for his son, or a desire for security.
But the contrast is unmistakable.
The man who went out from the presence of the LORD became associated with the first city-building recorded in Scripture.
A person can accomplish something extraordinary and still need to be reconciled to God.
That truth is as relevant now as it was in Genesis.
You can build a successful business and neglect your soul.
You can build a beautiful house and fill it with bitterness.
You can build an impressive reputation while hiding dishonesty.
You can even build a public religious identity while privately resisting the very Lord you speak about.
And the frightening part is that people may applaud what you have built without knowing what is happening inside you.
They see the city.
God sees the heart.
But we need to go deeper.
Because there is another Hebrew detail in this passage that makes the story even more striking.
Cain settled in the land of Nod.
The Hebrew name is written:
נוֹד — Nod
The name is associated with the Hebrew root נוד (nud), connected with wandering or restlessness.
Earlier, God had declared that Cain would be "a fugitive and a vagabond" in the earth (Genesis 4:12, KJV).
The Hebrew description includes:
נָע וָנָד — na va-nad
A wanderer and a restless fugitive.
Now notice the literary tension.
A man sentenced to wandering settles in a place whose name evokes wandering.
And there, he builds a city.
A place associated with permanence.
A place where people might gather, live, work, and establish families.
There is an almost painful irony in the narrative.
The wanderer builds a settlement.
The restless man establishes a place to remain.
But Genesis does not tell us that the city removed the consequences of his sin.
And here is the question that reaches beyond Cain.
What are you building because you are afraid to face what is happening in your soul?
Some people build careers to avoid confronting their loneliness.
Some build wealth to silence their insecurity.
Some build social-media identities because they cannot bear the thought of being ordinary.
Some keep themselves surrounded by noise because silence reminds them of things they have never surrendered to God.
And some remain endlessly active in ministry while quietly losing the intimacy with Christ that first made their service meaningful.
None of those activities is automatically sinful.
Work is not evil.
Success is not evil.
Cities are not evil.
Providing for your family is good.
Serving in ministry is good.
The danger comes when we begin asking created things to give us the peace, forgiveness, identity, and security that only God can ultimately provide.
Because a city cannot forgive sin.
A title cannot cleanse a conscience.
A bank account cannot resurrect a dead relationship.
And public admiration cannot make a guilty person righteous before God.
Cain's son was named Enoch.
In Hebrew:
חֲנוֹךְ — Chanokh
The name is commonly associated with dedication or inauguration, from the Hebrew root חנך (chanakh), meaning to dedicate or initiate.
Cain named the city after Enoch.
It was a name that could represent the continuation of his family line.
A future beyond the terrible events of the past.
But be careful not to confuse this Enoch with the later Enoch in Genesis 5, the descendant of Seth who walked with God and whom God took.
They were different men from different genealogical lines.
The Enoch of Genesis 4 was Cain's son.
The Enoch of Genesis 5 was the man Scripture describes as walking with God.
That contrast is worth remembering, though the Bible does not give us enough information to judge the spiritual condition of Cain's son Enoch.
We must not assign a father's guilt to a child.
And we must not assume that Cain's descendants were incapable of faith or moral responsibility.
The biblical text is more careful than that.
Yet there is something deeply human about naming a city after your child.
Parents know this feeling.
You look at your son or daughter and imagine a better future.
You hope they will avoid your mistakes.
You pray they will never carry the wounds you carry.
You want them to inherit something good.
Something lasting.
Something that says your life was not only defined by failure.
Perhaps Cain had hopes for Enoch. Scripture does not tell us.
But it invites a sobering question for every generation.
What are we leaving our children?
Only possessions?
Only achievements?
Only a family name?
Or are we also showing them what it looks like to humble ourselves before God?
A father can leave his child a city and still fail to leave an example of repentance.
A mother can provide every material comfort and still struggle to model forgiveness.
A family can be financially secure and spiritually starving.
And sometimes the greatest inheritance a child can receive is not a building, a business, or an estate.
It is the memory of a parent who knew how to say:
"I was wrong."
"Please forgive me."
"Let's pray."
"We need Jesus."
Because the Gospel does not teach that human achievement is worthless.
It teaches that human achievement cannot save us.
And that brings us to the most important part of this entire story.
Cain was a murderer.
But even after his crime, God did not permit others to kill him without consequence.
When Cain feared that someone would kill him, the LORD declared that vengeance would come upon anyone who killed him, and God appointed a sign for his protection (Genesis 4:13–15).
We do not know what that sign physically looked like.
Scripture does not describe its appearance.
And it certainly does not justify later racial interpretations that have been wrongly attached to the so-called mark of Cain.
What Scripture does reveal is that God's judgment was accompanied by restraint.
Cain was held accountable.
His sin was not excused.
Abel's blood was not forgotten.
Yet Cain's life was protected.
That is a difficult and powerful truth.
God's mercy does not mean sin is harmless, and God's judgment does not mean He has ceased to be merciful.
But do not confuse the protection Cain received with proof that he repented.
The Bible does not explicitly record Cain's repentance.
It does not tell us that Cain was spiritually restored.
And we should never claim more than Scripture reveals.
What we can say is that God's dealings with Cain display both the seriousness of sin and the reality of divine restraint.
Then the story moves forward.
Generations pass.
Human wickedness spreads.
Cities rise.
Kingdoms emerge.
And the Bible continues telling the story of a world desperately in need of redemption.
Until another Man enters history.
Not a man trying to escape the consequences of His own sin.
A Man who had no sin.
Not a man whose hands were stained with his brother's blood.
A Man who willingly shed His own blood to save sinners.
Jesus Christ.
And suddenly, the contrast becomes overwhelming.
Cain killed his brother.
Jesus laid down His life for those He came to save.
Cain's story includes blood crying out from the ground.
Jesus' story leads us to blood that speaks of a better covenant.
Hebrews 12:24 describes Jesus as:
"...the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel." (KJV)
Do not miss the beauty of that sentence.
Abel's blood testified to injustice.
The blood of Jesus secures redemption for those who come to God through Him.
The Greek expression in Hebrews 12:24 is:
κρεῖττον λαλοῦντι παρὰ τὸν Ἅβελ
Kreitton lalounti para ton Habel.
It speaks of something better than Abel.
The verse does not mean that Abel's murder was insignificant.
It means that Christ's sacrificial blood belongs to a greater and better covenant reality.
Hebrews is directing our attention to Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant.
The One whose sacrifice accomplishes what our efforts could never accomplish.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Cleansing.
Access to God.
And the promise of an eternal inheritance.
This is where the ancient city of Genesis 4 begins to point us toward a much larger biblical story.
Not because Cain's city was secretly a prophecy about Jesus.
Scripture never says that.
But because the Bible begins with humanity alienated by sin and moves toward God's gracious promise of dwelling with His redeemed people.
Cain built a city named after his son.
But Hebrews 11:10 tells us that Abraham looked for a city:
"...which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God." (KJV)
And Revelation 21 shows us the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven.
The story that began with human rebellion does not end with human beings successfully saving themselves.
It ends with God dwelling with His people.
Revelation 21:3 declares:
"Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God." (KJV)
Read that again.
Cain went out from the presence of the LORD.
But the final biblical vision of redemption is God dwelling with His people.
The contrast is breathtaking.
Humanity's deepest problem was never a shortage of buildings.
It was sin and separation from God.
And humanity's greatest hope is not a better civilization built by human hands.
It is reconciliation with the living God through Jesus Christ.
That is why the Gospel is not merely advice for becoming a better person.
It is the announcement of what God has accomplished through the death and resurrection of His Son.
Jesus died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day.
And through Him, forgiveness is proclaimed to sinners who repent and believe.
You do not have to pretend that your past never happened.
You do not have to decorate your shame until nobody recognizes it.
You do not have to spend the rest of your life trying to earn a forgiveness that only grace can give.
You need Christ.
Not because your failures are small.
But because His saving work is sufficient.
The apostle Paul wrote:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." (2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV)
In Greek, the central declaration is:
καινὴ κτίσις — kainē ktisis
A new creation.
Not merely a polished version of the old self.
Not simply a new reputation.
Not a carefully constructed image.
A new creation in Christ.
That does not mean the earthly consequences of our sins always disappear.
Forgiveness does not automatically rebuild trust.
Repentance does not remove every legal or relational responsibility.
Restoration may require confession, restitution, patience, accountability, and time.
But in Christ, the sinner is no longer required to seek salvation through self-reinvention.
Grace offers something far greater.
Reconciliation with God.
And a transformed life that begins with Him.
Maybe you have been trying to build your own version of Enoch.
A future impressive enough to distract everyone from your past.
A life busy enough to keep your conscience quiet.
A reputation polished enough that nobody asks what happened behind closed doors.
But what if the most important thing you need tonight is not another accomplishment?
What if it is an honest conversation with God?
Not a performance.
Not another religious promise you intend to break.
Just surrender.
"Lord, I have sinned."
"Lord, I have been hiding."
"Lord, I have been building everything except my relationship with You."
"Jesus, have mercy on me."
There is no shame in coming to Christ with the truth.
The shame is not what saves you.
Jesus saves.
And the same Savior who calls sinners to repentance also promises that those who come to Him will not be cast out (John 6:37).
Perhaps you are reading this with tears you have been holding back for years.
Perhaps you are a parent grieving mistakes you cannot undo.
Perhaps you are a believer who looks spiritually strong in public but feels distant from God in private.
Perhaps you are someone who has never truly surrendered to Jesus Christ.
Hear this carefully.
Your past matters.
Your choices matter.
The people you have hurt matter.
But your story does not have to remain a story of hiding, pride, and spiritual emptiness.
There is a Savior who died and rose again.
There is forgiveness in His name.
There is grace that teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
There is a new life that calls us away from sin and toward holiness.
And there is hope beyond what you have built or destroyed.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious words.
Not to turn Scripture into another passing social-media trend.
But to keep pointing wounded hearts, wandering believers, searching souls, and struggling families toward the truth of Jesus Christ.
If this message has exposed something you have been carrying, do not rush past that conviction.
Take a moment to pray.
Not as a formula for salvation.
Not to prove your faith to strangers.
But as an honest expression of what God is stirring in your heart.
There are battles that should not be fought alone.

And if Christ has already brought you through a season of shame, failure, or restoration, share a little of your testimony. Someone who believes their life is beyond redemption may need to hear how the Lord met you in yours.
There is also a deeper way to walk alongside this mission.

We want those resources to keep reaching people who cannot afford to purchase books, who are rebuilding their faith, who are searching for biblical answers, or who simply need encouragement to open God's Word again.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not a promise that giving money will purchase God's favor.
But willing partnership in a mission you believe is worth sustaining.
Someone who may never know your name.
Someone in another city.
Another country.
Another season of suffering.
Someone who might open a Gospel Warrior article at the very moment they are beginning to lose hope.
It is the opportunity to help keep Christ-centered biblical teaching and free discipleship resources available to people who need them.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite your family and friends to read it.
Your prayers, encouragement, and willingness to share the truth matter.
Because the Gospel is not merchandise.
The Gospel is good news.
And the good news must never be held hostage to a payment.
Now, before you leave, return with me one final time to Genesis 4.
A man named Cain.
A son named Enoch.
A city rising in the land of Nod.
And a terrible history that no human construction could erase.
Thousands of years later, people are still doing what Cain's story warns us about.
Building.
Achieving.
Expanding.
Collecting.
Trying to make a name that will survive them.
But eventually, every human life must face a question more important than what we accomplished.
Were we reconciled to God?
Because one day the applause will stop.
The accounts will close.
The buildings will belong to someone else.
The names on the walls will fade.
And everything we once thought made us important will be seen in the light of eternity.
But those who belong to Jesus Christ have a hope that no earthly city can provide.
A Savior who has conquered death.
A forgiveness purchased by His blood.
A future secured by His resurrection.
And a home prepared by the One who will never abandon His redeemed people.
So build responsibly.
Work faithfully.
Love your family.
Serve your community.
Use whatever God has entrusted to you for His glory.
But never mistake what you build for the One who saves.
And never let the pursuit of leaving your name on something become more important than belonging to Jesus Christ.
Cain's city reminds us how much a person can build after a tragedy.
The Gospel reminds us that only Christ can redeem sinners and give them new life.
And perhaps that is the truth your heart needed today.
You can spend your whole life building a place for your name to be remembered—and still miss the grace of the Savior who calls you to come home.
